Because failure is an option SpaceX can do stuff like land rockets on a boat

This is an argument I have struggled to make in space advocacy circles for many years. The high cost of space activity is a product of a compulsion to increase intrinsic risk. Elon Musk can innovate because he can afford to take big risks. Good for him. But that's only one approach. We can also innovate by managing the risk itself. Payload values drive launch costs by compelling engineering to go to expensive lengths to insure it. We stick payloads on rockets whose intrinsic values are equivalent to an entire automobile manufacturing plant (or higher, if it's state hero/astronauts), which makes failure untenable, and which then demands going to incredible lengths to make rockets--machines that run on a controlled explosion to achieve incredible velocities--achieve near-perfect reliability to safeguard those payloads. No one questions why the hell the payloads are so valuable in the first place and what me might do about that.

In industry failure is not only an option, it's routine. Most industry runs on a principle of 'tolerable yield'--an acceptance that production always results in a certain amount of failure that you try to keep tolerable relative to marginal costs. As long as the unit cost is modest, a modest rate of production failure is tolerable. So power companies accept a 1/3 loss of energy produced to losses in the municipal grid, microprocessor manufacturers accept a loss of, sometimes, up to half their production, and so on in just about ever industry. They all have some tolerable margin of loss relative to marginal cost.

But, because space activity started out as a geopolitical competition, every early payload had a nation's prestige attached to it. It became a national treasure. Like launching the freakin' Mona Lisa to space. And every astronaut was a national hero whose loss could mean a month or more of national mourning exploited by the news media and officials being publicly vilified and losing their careers. We can use-up the lives of all sorts of low-class workers as though they were match sticks, but dead astronauts matter. So just as you aren't likely to haul the Mona Lisa around in the average Post Office truck, we weren't leaving anything to chance with these kinds of payloads. And the aerospace industry seemed to get trapped in this mentality, developers of satellites falling into this habit of creating, as I call them, Faberge Eggs--impossibly precious and expensive one-off artifacts--and then expecting the rockets to secure that ridiculous risk. And that compels a hyper-conservatism in launch systems design and development. it's hard to innovate when there's always too much monetary (or geopolitical) risk. Only people like Elon Musk can afford that risk--and there simply never will be enough of such people.

So I've long argued that the key to economizing on the access to space rests in figuring out how to make value out there rather than sending it there to reduce the cost of launch by reducing the intrinsic risk of space transportation. We have to question why we're making and putting Faberge Eggs on rockets. And one emerging tool for lowering the value of payloads is telereobotics, which allows us to increasingly make stuff on orbit and reduce payloads to stuff of lower value; commodity parts and bulk materials. The cheaper it is to experiment, the more experimenting we can do, and that's how you get innovation.

I think an issue you're not considering is capitalism. Capitalism would work incredibly well if companies would agree to just compete against each other and grind their prices down until one simply could not afford to do lower them anymore and the consumer reaped all the benefits. In reality most relevant industries today have major barriers to entry and competition, and instead of grinding each other down the few big players acknowledge they can make a lot more money by colluding than they can by competing.

Before SpaceX we still had a completely free market in rocketry, but the natural barriers to entry meant that there were only really a handful of meaningful players including Lockheed Martin and Boeing. And these companies did not really accomplish much of anything. Until recently we were still using soviet era technology to launch rockets - not just technology developed during soviet times but at times literally technology built during the soviet era. What did change is the price of launches. Under this oligopoly prices for launches skyrocketed. The final per-launch cost for the Space Shuttle ended up in excess of $1.5 billion dollars!! That's really just completely out of touch with reality in the same way many costs in our economy are out of touch with reality.

While I think Musk is undoubtedly brilliant, he's also unique in simply playing in capitalism like it was meant to be played but that's clearly since he's guided by something beyond just the accumulation of wealth. Most people that find themselves with the sort of wealth he has only got there because of a steadfast obsession with the accumulation of wealth itself. As opposed to a means to an end, the wealth is the ends in and of itself for them. The same is also true in the electric car market. What Elon did with Tesla is undoubtedly amazing, but these other companies have had decades they could have been working on this. Innovation and competition cost money - whereas complacency and collusion create money.

Basically I don't necessarily think this whole thing is an issue just of this particular market - it's an issue of capitalism in general. If we could find more individuals with the means and desire to achieve greater things than just the accumulation of wealth I think we could see similar revolutions in an absurd number of industries in the US.

I'm in general agreement with the points you make. Aerospace development has not really seen the kind of open competition that you would expect from free market development, perhaps because of its interdependence with military defence and national space agencies. That may be a key reason why we haven't seen the rise of a more logical paradigm in systems development akin to that of normal industries. Most-certainly, Musk is not typical for his social class. He definitely is a 'space cadet' and that affords him a drive beyond the usual economic rationalizations. There was never a 'boom' in space investment akin to the Dotcom Boom. The ROI was always tenuous. So true entrepreneurs needed more than economic reasons to get into the field of space development.

So I'd never thought of it exactly like this before but capitalism is based on the assumption that both prisoners defect, and it's built to maximize the overall outcome of this case.
